compounding_issues: Session 5 changed the public GET /tasks contract from a bare array to a paginated envelope {"data", "next_cursor", "total"}, invalidating every existing list-task test and forcing a mass test rewrite late in the story

Session 3 introduced a hardcoded Redis dependency (Celery broker/backend at localhost:6379) that session 5's Flask-Limiter storage then doubled down on, making Redis a mandatory runtime service rather than an isolated concern
Session 4's refactor was partial — schema/migration logic (get_db, init_db, migrate) stayed in app.py while data access moved to repositories, splitting data-layer responsibility across two modules
Session 2's JWT auth carried the default 'dev-secret-change-me' SECRET_KEY and hardcoded token expiry forward, leaving a security smell that was never addressed by later sessions
Greenfield session 1 added no implementation at all (the seed was already complete) — it only authored tests, so the story's first substantive build step actually happened in session 2
key_decisions: Adopting JWT auth with owner_id scoping in session 2 — every task query became owner-filtered, and this invariant cleanly propagated through the repository layer, pagination, and rate-limiting keying in later sessions
Decoupling notification delivery via Celery async tasks (send_notification_email.delay) rather than in-request work, giving session 3 a clean integration seam
Extracting a BaseRepository abstract class + TaskRepository/UserRepository in session 4, keeping all 32 tests green (a behavior-preserving refactor)
Using JWT-user-derived keys instead of IP addresses for Flask-Limiter rate limiting, plus a shared scope so GET/POST count together toward the same per-user budget
Choosing cursor/keyset pagination (id < cursor ORDER BY id DESC) instead of offset pagination for scalable large-list reads
Building an idempotent migrate() with PRAGMA-guarded ALTER TABLEs to evolve the SQLite schema without destroying existing data
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily and monotonically. Sessions 1-3 grew feature breadth with tests growing 12 → 26 → 32, all green; session 4 was a disciplined, test-preserving structural refactor (32 → 32, zero regressions); session 5 was the story's peak of difficulty and cost — 79 tool calls, 9 retries, 820s, roughly 4x the budget of earlier sessions — with visible struggle against Flask-Limiter 4.x mocking and scope semantics, yet it still finished green at 43 tests with genuinely harder cross-cutting features. The only quality wobble was the deliberate breaking change to the list endpoint's response shape, which cost real rework but was contained. The arc is one of competence rising with task difficulty: the agent handled harder integration and refactor work more confidently, and only the final ops-hardening session stretched it.
story_review.summary: A textbook incremental build — greenfield → auth → async integration → repository refactor → cross-cutting ops — that stayed test-green at every commit and grew in sophistication and difficulty with each session, marred only by a late breaking API-contract change and a couple of lingering infrastructure coupling choices.
